newsitem.title: HONG KONG: No day of rest for the crew of Sir Percivale.
newsitem.headline: No day of rest for the crew of Sir Percivale.

text.p: Sunday was no day of rest for the hardworking crew of the Royal Fleet Auxiliary ship Sir Percivale who are racing against the clock to complete the final phase of Britain's historic military pullout from Hong Kong.
With just nine days to go before the curtain falls on Britain's 156-year presence in Hong Kong, the tank deck of the supply and troop ship is quickly filling up.

The British garrison in Hong Kong had no tanks to shift home -- the incoming Chinese military is also not expected to deploy tanks here -- but there is plenty of equipment to be moved before the last British troops leave carrying little more than hand-baggage.
Mobile kitchens, generators and the live broadcast van used by the British Forces radio station in Hong Kong, carefully labelled and crated, were neatly stowed.

Crane operators carefully lowered wooden boxes of small arms, office furniture and sports equipment from the garrison's Prince of Wales Barracks on Hong Kong Island and from Osborn Barracks on the Kowloon peninsula which closed last month.

One of the last loads to be stowed at almost the very last minute will be the ammunition issued to what remains of the British garrison, now down to fewer than 1,000 men and women, from around 9,000 only three years earlier.

The grey amphibious landing and logistics ship is docked at Stonecutters' Island in the middle of Victoria Harbour, near the locked and shuttered Tamar Naval base, decommissioned in April when the Royal Navy lowered its ensign over the last British naval base east of Suez.
The roll-on roll-off merchantman will remain there until the handover when it will join a flotilla led by the Royal Yacht Britannia, said Sir Perivale's First Officer Martin Jones..

Britannia will carry away Price Charles and the last Governor of Hong Kong, Chris Patten, after the British flag is lowered for the last time at midnight on June 30 and the red flag of China flutters over the territory of 6.4 million people.
"Britannia will be followed by the frigate HMS Chatham, then comes the three Royal Naval Patrol craft, Peacock, Starling and Plover, and then us," Jones added.

The three patrol ships have been sold to the Philippine navy and Sir Percivale will accompany them on their last voyage to Manila. The British crew will transfer to the RFA ship, which can carry up to 350 troops, said Jones.

Jones, who is in charge of supplies and logistics and served for nearly two years off the town of Split supporting United Nations troops in the former Yugoslavia, said Sir Percivale will head from the Philippines to the Maldives, pass through the Suez canal, call in at Corfu and northern Spain before arriving back in Southampton, England on August 28.
It will not be carrying the remaining garrison troops of the Black Watch regiment. They will be flying out.
After the handover, Hong Kong will become a quasi-autonomous capitalist region of China, and China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) will take over defence responsibilities.
An advance party of nearly 200 PLA troops are already in Hong Kong preparing facilities for the incoming garrison.

The Sir Percivale saw action during the 1982 Falklands War when Britain routed Argentine invasion forces from the south Atlantic colony, and in the 1991 Gulf War when an international coalition drove Iraqi invasion forces from Kuwait.
